text: Have them bring a young bull and a grain offering of choice flour moistened with olive oil, along with a second young bull for a sin offering.

content:
We have been walking through Numbers 8 together; the cleansing of the Levites, the water, the razor, the washed garments. We have seen how those three acts of purification speak to us as New Creation believers. Now, after the cleansing was complete, Yahweh's instructions did not stop there. The Levites were brought forward, and two young bulls were prepared; one as a burnt offering with a grain offering of choice flour moistened with olive oil, and a second young bull as a sin offering. Two animals. Two distinct acts.

And together they carry a message that takes our breath away when we see what they are pointing to. We will come to the grain offering tomorrow. Today we look at the two bulls; and what Yahweh was showing us when He required them both.

When we first read that two bulls were required for the consecration of the Levites, it is easy to pass over this as simply another requirement of the Law. But every detail in the tabernacle instructions was chosen by Yahweh with precision, and the two bulls are no exception. Each animal had a completely different purpose, and together they represent two things that cannot happen in the wrong order. The first bull mentioned in the text was for the burnt offering. The second bull mentioned was for the sin offering. But here is something we must notice carefully: even though the sin offering is called the second bull in the way the text introduces them, it was actually offered first in the ceremony. Numbers 8:12 makes this plain; the sin offering came before the burnt offering. So why is it named second but acted upon first?

The answer is simple but instructive. The Torah often introduces things in the order they are described, not necessarily in the order they are used. The first bull is mentioned first because it represents the higher purpose; the total consecration, the sweet-smelling surrender to Yahweh. But before that could happen, something else had to be dealt with first. The sin offering had to come before the burnt offering. This is not a technicality. It is a deeply important truth that runs through the entire Levitical system. You cannot offer yourself wholly to Yahweh while sin still stands between you and Him. Defilement must be addressed before dedication can be accepted.

The Levites laid their hands on the head of the sin offering bull. This was not a casual gesture. In the Levitical system, the laying on of hands was the act of identification and transfer. The one who pressed his hands on the animal's head was saying: this animal now stands in my place. What belongs to me; my guilt, my defilement, my unworthiness is being placed on this animal. And then the animal was slain. It bore what the offerer deserved, and it died under that weight. The sin offering did not go up to Yahweh as a sweet aroma. It was not a gift ascending in fragrance. It was a payment; the settling of a debt that the Levite could not settle himself.

This is a portrait of Calvary. When Christwas nailed to the wood, He was not there as an example or a teacher. He was there as the sin offering. Everything that was wrong with us; every sin, every defilement, every reason why we could not approach a holy Yahweh, was laid upon Him. Isaiah saw this and wrote it centuries before it happened: "Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). Paul put it even more plainly: "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us" (A sin offering for us) (2 Corinthians 5:21). Just as the Levite pressed his hands on the second bull and his guilt passed to that animal, so our faith lays hold of what Christ did at Calvary; and our guilt passes to Him.
He becomes the bearer. He becomes the substitute. He goes down under the weight of what we deserved.

Calvary was not a beautiful moment in the way the world understands beauty. It was dark and heavy; the full weight of divine judgment falling on the One who had done nothing to deserve it. It was the moment when the holy Son of Yahweh bore the unholy weight of all that we were. The Hebrew word used for what the sin offering accomplished is kipper; to cover, to cancel, to wipe clean. That is what happened at Calvary. The barrier between us and Yahweh; guilt, condemnation, the broken record of every wrong thing was completely removed. Paul says it simply and powerfully: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). That is the second bull. That is what had to happen first.

Now here is where the picture deepens in a way that is truly remarkable.
The first bull; the burnt offering was named first in the text. And that naming tells us something important about Christ that we must not miss. From the very moment of his consecration at baptism in the Jordan river, Christ had already given himself wholly to Yahweh. His entire life from that day forward was a burnt offering in motion. Every step he took, every word he spoke, every act of obedience in private and in public, every night spent in prayer on the hillside all of it was a life being continually poured out, completely and without reservation, to his Father. He did not begin his dedication at the cross. It began at the water. The burnt offering was already ascending from the moment Yahweh's voice declared over him: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). From his baptism to Gethsemane, from Gethsemane to Golgotha; the first bull was always first in that sense. It describes who Christ was throughout his consecrated life.

But then comes the mystery that the two bulls together reveal. Even though Christ had lived a wholly dedicated life from his baptism onward, when he came to the cross; the moment of his final and complete self-offering; the sin offering had to stand first. The second bull had to be acted upon before the burnt offering could fully ascend and be accepted. This is not a contradiction. It is a profound truth. Christ could not present the complete offering of his consecrated life to Yahweh without first passing through the sin offering.

Our sin stood in the way. Our guilt had to be removed before his total self-giving could reach its final and fullest expression before the Father. The cross was therefore not the beginning of his dedication; it was the moment when his lifetime of consecration passed through the sin offering and came out the other side, complete, accepted, and crowned. The second bull becoming first at the altar shows us this: even the most perfectly consecrated life cannot be fully received by Yahweh while our sin remains undealt with. And so Christ, who had no sin of his own, took ours; so that the burnt offering of his life could ascend without hindrance, wholly and finally, to the Father who had always been pleased with him.

Paul holds both realities together in one sentence: "He gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to Yahweh" (Ephesians 5:2). The fragrance went up to the Father even while the judgment came down upon the sin He was carrying. Both movements; downward and upward happened at the same moment, on the same cross. Two bulls. One sacrifice. Both fulfilled completely, and in the right order.

There is one more thing we must carry away from this. The order is fixed and cannot be reversed; not for the Levites, and not for us. Atonement must come before dedication. The sin offering must come before the burnt offering.

No amount of sincere personal dedication can substitute for the clearing of sin. A person who tries to offer themselves wholly to Yahweh while the barrier of guilt still stands between them cannot complete that offering. The burnt offering can only ascend when the sin offering has first done its work. In our own lives this means we do not begin with consecration. We begin at the cross. We receive the atonement that Christ provided as the sin offering. We let the barrier be removed. And then; standing on cleared ground, justified and forgiven, we are able to offer ourselves as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to Yahweh (Romans 12:1). Not before. After. This is the pattern Yahweh built into the wilderness tabernacle, and it is the pattern He has not changed.

Tomorrow we will look at the grain offering of choice flour moistened with olive oil ;and we will see yet another layer of what Yahweh so carefully prepared in that wilderness camp. But for today, let us sit with the weight and the wonder of the two bulls. Two animals. Two offerings. One perfect sacrifice. A consecrated life that began at baptism, passed through the sin offering at Calvary, and was received by the Father in its fullness once and for all.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We stand before You today with nothing of our own to offer

except what You Yourself have made possible.

You required two bulls and, in Your wisdom, and love,

You provided in Your Son what we could never have provided ourselves.

A life wholly given from the day of his baptism the burnt offering ascending.

A cross where the sin offering stood first, the barrier removed, the debt settled.

And then his consecrated life received in its fullness, complete and accepted.

Let us never treat that lightly. Let it always move us.

And having received the atonement, may we now offer ourselves

wholly, without reservation; as those who stand on cleared ground.

I will praise You, O Yahweh, with my whole heart;

I will declare all Your marvellous works. Psalm 9:1

We ask this in the name of the perfect sacrifice, our Christ.
